trades-reset-1.title: Job 01 · Make a fitted notebook tray
trades-reset-1.bodyHtml:
The job

A paper tray that fits your closed pocket notebook, built by a partner from your work order.

110 minutes / two periods. Project-based vocational mathematics. Chromebook guides six stages; pocket notebook holds drawings, measurements, calculations, test results, and revisions. Three selected digital responses; no duplicate digital drawing required.

Prepare

Per student: pocket notebook, tape measure, pencil, about 3 sheets of letter paper. Per pair: scissors and a straightedge or folder edge; shared tape.

Make one sample tray. Project the pattern or print the two-page student job. Optional nonzero-start check: a tape reads 1 in at one end and 4 5/8 in at the other; length = 3 5/8 in.

Learning evidence

  1. I can measure from stated endpoints, record units and resolution, and check a reading.
  2. I can calculate lengths, clearances, area, and perimeter with appropriate units.
  3. I can make a dimensioned drawing or work order another person can use.
  4. I can use a fit or inspection result to make and explain a revision.

Use direct observation for tool action and product/drawing evidence. Digital saves and XP are participation records, not mastery ratings. First two jobs establish a baseline: independent / with cue / not observed. Keep existing grading policy; do not turn a group product into every student’s individual rating.

110-minute sequence

  1. 0–15 min · Brief: Put your notebook on the desk. What must another person know to make a tray that fits it? On scrap paper mark 2 3/8 in, then explain which tick is 1/8 in on your tape. This is a starting check, not a grade.
  2. 15–27 min · Measure: Close your notebook. Sketch its cover, label length L and width W, and mark the endpoints you will use. Keep the tape straight and read to the nearest 1/16 in if your tape allows.
  3. 27–55 min · Plan: Calculate both base dimensions for YOUR notebook with 1/8 in clearance on each side. Add two 3/4 in walls to each base dimension to find your outer blank.
  4. 55–78 min · Make: Mark the outer blank on paper and check both dimensions. Cut only the outside rectangle.
  5. 78–99 min · Test: Return the tray to its owner. Insert and remove the closed notebook three times without forcing or tearing. Check that the notebook lies flat and that the tray base is not bowed.
  6. 99–110 min · Explain: Complete the individual exit below before discussing answers.

Brief

  1. Put your notebook on the desk. What must another person know to make a tray that fits it? On scrap paper mark 2 3/8 in, then explain which tick is 1/8 in on your tape. This is a starting check, not a grade.
  2. Set up a dated notebook spread: sketch and readings on the left; calculation, decision, test, and revision on the right. Mark small sketches NTS unless drawn to a chosen scale.
  3. Work in pairs and rotate roles. Each student keeps an individual notebook and performs a tool action and a calculation.

Notebook: Write the job title, date, user/purpose, and your prediction. Keep the Chromebook on the desk while you measure or build.

Measure

  1. Close your notebook. Sketch its cover, label length L and width W, and mark the endpoints you will use. Keep the tape straight and read to the nearest 1/16 in if your tape allows.
  2. Measure L and W yourself. Write units and tape resolution. Your partner checks the same endpoints with their tape; remeasure disagreements before choosing the values for your design.
  3. Keep your original readings. Circle the dimensions you will use; explain any change. The object is your closed notebook, not the worked-example notebook.

Notebook: Record readings, endpoints/reference, units, and source. Label values measured, supplied, calculated, or assumed.

Plan

  1. Calculate both base dimensions for YOUR notebook with 1/8 in clearance on each side. Add two 3/4 in walls to each base dimension to find your outer blank.
  2. Draw an NTS plan in your notebook. On a separate scrap, write a work order: owner, builder, base L/W, blank L/W, wall height, units, and a labeled sketch. Check that the blank fits your paper before cutting; join sheets if needed.
  3. Swap work orders. Ask one clarification before building. Keep your notebook calculation; your partner builds from the scrap.

Notebook: Show operations with units, a labeled drawing, and your work order or decision. Keep original and revised work readable.

Make

  1. Mark the outer blank on paper and check both dimensions. Cut only the outside rectangle.
  2. Mark fold lines 3/4 in from all four edges. Keep the corner squares. From the TOP and BOTTOM edges, cut along the two vertical fold lines only as far as the first horizontal fold line: four short slits total.
  3. Fold all four walls upward. Fold each corner tab inward and tape it to the neighboring wall. Keep the base flat. This tray stays supported on the desk; do not carry the notebook in it.

Notebook: Record a build issue or clarification as it occurs. Your product and notebook are the work for this stage.

Test

  1. Return the tray to its owner. Insert and remove the closed notebook three times without forcing or tearing. Check that the notebook lies flat and that the tray base is not bowed.
  2. Compare the built base dimensions with the work order. Record one actual observation, then revise a fold, tab, dimension, or unclear work-order label. Retest and record what changed.
  3. If it already fits, keep the dimensions and improve a communication detail. A successful first attempt still needs evidence.

Notebook: Record requirement → test/reading → decision → revision → retest. Keep unexpected results; do not invent success.

Explain

  1. Complete the individual exit below before discussing answers.
  2. Add the test result, revision, and notebook page reference to your response. Use the notebook as evidence rather than retyping every page.
  3. Save the three selected responses and submit the lesson for teacher review. Show your physical work and notebook to the teacher. Clean up and return shared supplies.

Notebook: Use your own calculation and observed evidence. If you used a supplied-data alternative, say so.

Worked vocational math

A model notebook is 5 1/2 in long and 3 1/2 in wide. Leave 1/8 in clear on EACH side and use 3/4 in walls. What blank is needed?

Inside base = notebook dimension + 2 × side clearance. Blank = inside base + 2 × wall height.

L: 5 1/2 + 1/4 = 5 3/4 in base; + 1 1/2 = 7 1/4 in blank. W: 3 1/2 + 1/4 = 3 3/4 in base; + 1 1/2 = 5 1/4 in blank.

Digital checkpoints

  1. Enter YOUR closed notebook length and width in inches, the tape resolution, and whether the partner check agreed. Record full readings and the sketch in your notebook.
  2. Enter YOUR planned inside base L × W and outer blank L × W, with units. Show one dimension calculation using two 1/8-in gaps and two 3/4-in walls. Keep the complete work order and drawing on paper.
  3. Work independently. A notebook is 3 7/8 in wide. With 1/8 in clearance on EACH side and 3/4 in walls, calculate base width and blank width. Show both operations and units. If you add only one wall, how far too narrow is the blank? Finish with one observed result from YOUR tray and the revision or check you made.

Teacher answer key and interpretation

Base = 4 1/8 in; blank = 5 5/8 in. Missing one wall makes the blank 3/4 in too narrow. Accept a test observation and justified retained dimension; do not require invented failure. Baseline: mark independent / with cue / not observed for reading, calculation, handoff, revision.

Inspect, support, extend

  1. Return the tray to its owner. Insert and remove the closed notebook three times without forcing or tearing. Check that the notebook lies flat and that the tray base is not bowed.
  2. Compare the built base dimensions with the work order. Record one actual observation, then revise a fold, tab, dimension, or unclear work-order label. Retest and record what changed.
  3. If it already fits, keep the dimensions and improve a communication detail. A successful first attempt still needs evidence.

Support: Use a fraction strip and say: notebook + gap + gap, then base + wall + wall. Demonstrate one paper corner with oversized folds.

Extension: Can two 7 1/4 × 5 1/4 in blanks fit on one 8 1/2 × 11 in sheet? Draw the orientation and verify each total.

Individual review

Look for: a checked tool reading; a justified calculation with units; a usable drawing/product; a test-based decision. Record missing evidence as not observed. Give one actionable next step and a chance to revise. Use the phase performance task for a later individual conference.

trades-reset-1.title: Job 02 · Survey one school zone
trades-reset-1.bodyHtml:
The job

A notebook survey another pair can use to locate three features.

110 minutes / two periods. Project-based vocational mathematics. Chromebook guides six stages; pocket notebook holds drawings, measurements, calculations, test results, and revisions. Three selected digital responses; no duplicate digital drawing required.

Prepare

Tapes, notebooks, pencils, loose paper; teacher-selected classroom or hallway zones.

Choose zones without interfering with doors, stairs, or normal circulation. Do not require students to enter restricted spaces.

Learning evidence

  1. I can measure from stated endpoints, record units and resolution, and check a reading.
  2. I can calculate lengths, clearances, area, and perimeter with appropriate units.
  3. I can make a dimensioned drawing or work order another person can use.
  4. I can use a fit or inspection result to make and explain a revision.

Use direct observation for tool action and product/drawing evidence. Digital saves and XP are participation records, not mastery ratings. First two jobs establish a baseline: independent / with cue / not observed. Keep existing grading policy; do not turn a group product into every student’s individual rating.

110-minute sequence

  1. 0–12 min · Brief: Estimate a desk width, then measure it. Convert 3 ft 4 in to inches. Why must every survey name a starting point?
  2. 12–30 min · Measure: Choose a reachable rectangular zone and draw an NTS plan. Name one fixed corner A as the datum and mark two directions from it.
  3. 30–50 min · Plan: Build one dimension string with at least three segments and compare its sum to the direct overall measurement.
  4. 50–78 min · Make: Exchange drawings with another pair. Use only their drawing to locate the three features.
  5. 78–98 min · Test: The receiving pair can identify all three features and the datum.
  6. 98–110 min · Explain: Complete the individual exit below before discussing answers.

Brief

  1. Estimate a desk width, then measure it. Convert 3 ft 4 in to inches. Why must every survey name a starting point?
  2. Set up a dated notebook spread: sketch and readings on the left; calculation, decision, test, and revision on the right. Mark small sketches NTS unless drawn to a chosen scale.
  3. Work in pairs and rotate roles. Each student keeps an individual notebook and performs a tool action and a calculation.

Notebook: Write the job title, date, user/purpose, and your prediction. Keep the Chromebook on the desk while you measure or build.

Measure

  1. Choose a reachable rectangular zone and draw an NTS plan. Name one fixed corner A as the datum and mark two directions from it.
  2. Measure two boundaries and locate three features from A. Each student takes at least one measurement. Label whether a dimension goes to an edge or center.
  3. Independently remeasure one boundary. Record both readings, the difference, and the resolution of the tape. Keep people moving through the hallway.

Notebook: Record readings, endpoints/reference, units, and source. Label values measured, supplied, calculated, or assumed.

Plan

  1. Build one dimension string with at least three segments and compare its sum to the direct overall measurement.
  2. Write the discrepancy with units. Decide which endpoint or reading needs checking; do not force the numbers to agree.
  3. Prepare a clean drawing with datum, orientation, three features, endpoints, and units. Mark NTS unless you deliberately draw to scale.

Notebook: Show operations with units, a labeled drawing, and your work order or decision. Keep original and revised work readable.

Make

  1. Exchange drawings with another pair. Use only their drawing to locate the three features.
  2. Mark an unclear endpoint or missing dimension on a separate review slip. Return it to the author.
  3. Remeasure as needed and issue a revised drawing with date and revision letter.

Notebook: Record a build issue or clarification as it occurs. Your product and notebook are the work for this stage.

Test

  1. The receiving pair can identify all three features and the datum.
  2. Overall length and segment sum are both shown, with any discrepancy explained at the tape resolution.
  3. Each student shows one actual tape reading to the teacher.

Notebook: Record requirement → test/reading → decision → revision → retest. Keep unexpected results; do not invent success.

Explain

  1. Complete the individual exit below before discussing answers.
  2. Add the test result, revision, and notebook page reference to your response. Use the notebook as evidence rather than retyping every page.
  3. Save the three selected responses and submit the lesson for teacher review. Show your physical work and notebook to the teacher. Clean up and return shared supplies.

Notebook: Use your own calculation and observed evidence. If you used a supplied-data alternative, say so.

Worked vocational math

Along a wall, two segments measure 2 ft 8 in and 3 ft 7 in. Find their combined length in feet/inches and inches.

Total inches = 12 × feet + inches; add in a common unit.

32 + 43 = 75 in = 6 ft 3 in.

Digital checkpoints

  1. Record one critical dimension or quantity for this job, with units, endpoints/reference or condition, and its source (measured or supplied). Give your check or one uncertainty. Add the notebook page/date so your teacher can find the full record.
  2. Share one calculation that controls YOUR job: the given values, operation, answer with units, and what the answer tells your builder or inspector. Use your actual design or the assigned classroom case; identify the source. Keep the full drawing and work in your notebook.
  3. A surveyed boundary is 8 ft 3 in. Two segments are 31 in and 42 in. Find the missing segment in inches and feet/inches. Name one change that made your survey easier to use.

Teacher answer key and interpretation

Overall 99 in; missing 99 − 31 − 42 = 26 in = 2 ft 2 in. Evidence must name an actual drawing change.

Inspect, support, extend

  1. The receiving pair can identify all three features and the datum.
  2. Overall length and segment sum are both shown, with any discrepancy explained at the tape resolution.
  3. Each student shows one actual tape reading to the teacher.

Support: Use inches first and a 12-in-to-1-ft reference. Give a partially drawn datum corner.

Extension: Draw the zone at 1 graph square = 6 in and recover two real dimensions from the drawing.

Individual review

Look for: a checked tool reading; a justified calculation with units; a usable drawing/product; a test-based decision. Record missing evidence as not observed. Give one actionable next step and a chance to revise. Use the phase performance task for a later individual conference.

trades-reset-1.title: Job 03 · Lay out a work area
trades-reset-1.bodyHtml:
The job

A full-size paper-marker footprint with checked sides, centers, and diagonals.

110 minutes / two periods. Project-based vocational mathematics. Chromebook guides six stages; pocket notebook holds drawings, measurements, calculations, test results, and revisions. Three selected digital responses; no duplicate digital drawing required.

Prepare

Tapes, notebooks, scrap-paper corner markers, approved removable tape if available; clear classroom floor.

Use loose paper markers if tape is not permitted. Keep the layout inside the approved area.

Learning evidence

  1. I can measure from stated endpoints, record units and resolution, and check a reading.
  2. I can calculate lengths, clearances, area, and perimeter with appropriate units.
  3. I can make a dimensioned drawing or work order another person can use.
  4. I can use a fit or inspection result to make and explain a revision.

Use direct observation for tool action and product/drawing evidence. Digital saves and XP are participation records, not mastery ratings. First two jobs establish a baseline: independent / with cue / not observed. Keep existing grading policy; do not turn a group product into every student’s individual rating.

110-minute sequence

  1. 0–12 min · Brief: A rectangular footprint must fit a proposed piece of equipment. Is checking two sides enough to establish a rectangle? Sketch a skewed counterexample.
  2. 12–30 min · Measure: Inspect the available floor area and mark a datum corner. Use a classroom model footprint 36 × 48 in, or a teacher-approved smaller version.
  3. 30–50 min · Plan: Calculate the center and two proposed fixture points 12 in from the short ends along the middle line.
  4. 50–78 min · Make: Lay out the center and fixture locations with small paper markers.
  5. 78–98 min · Test: For this classroom exercise, sides must be within 1/4 in of the requested lengths and each diagonal within 1/4 in of 60 in; this is an assigned model tolerance.
  6. 98–110 min · Explain: Complete the individual exit below before discussing answers.

Brief

  1. A rectangular footprint must fit a proposed piece of equipment. Is checking two sides enough to establish a rectangle? Sketch a skewed counterexample.
  2. Set up a dated notebook spread: sketch and readings on the left; calculation, decision, test, and revision on the right. Mark small sketches NTS unless drawn to a chosen scale.
  3. Work in pairs and rotate roles. Each student keeps an individual notebook and performs a tool action and a calculation.

Notebook: Write the job title, date, user/purpose, and your prediction. Keep the Chromebook on the desk while you measure or build.

Measure

  1. Inspect the available floor area and mark a datum corner. Use a classroom model footprint 36 × 48 in, or a teacher-approved smaller version.
  2. Mark the four corners with paper markers. Measure all four sides and both diagonals, keeping the tape straight.
  3. Write actual measurements; distinguish the intended 36/48 dimensions from your readings.

Notebook: Record readings, endpoints/reference, units, and source. Label values measured, supplied, calculated, or assumed.

Plan

  1. Calculate the center and two proposed fixture points 12 in from the short ends along the middle line.
  2. Write coordinates from the same datum. Make a sketch another pair can follow.
  3. Use the ideal 60-in diagonal as a check for the 36 × 48 in model, not as a substitute for measuring the sides.

Notebook: Show operations with units, a labeled drawing, and your work order or decision. Keep original and revised work readable.

Make

  1. Lay out the center and fixture locations with small paper markers.
  2. A second pair measures all sides and diagonals independently.
  3. Adjust the corners and recheck after each move. Leave a before/after reading in the notebook.

Notebook: Record a build issue or clarification as it occurs. Your product and notebook are the work for this stage.

Test

  1. For this classroom exercise, sides must be within 1/4 in of the requested lengths and each diagonal within 1/4 in of 60 in; this is an assigned model tolerance.
  2. Show the datum, both fixture coordinates, and the final center.
  3. Explain why a matching pair of diagonals alone does not prove that the requested side dimensions are correct.

Notebook: Record requirement → test/reading → decision → revision → retest. Keep unexpected results; do not invent success.

Explain

  1. Complete the individual exit below before discussing answers.
  2. Add the test result, revision, and notebook page reference to your response. Use the notebook as evidence rather than retyping every page.
  3. Save the three selected responses and submit the lesson for teacher review. Show your physical work and notebook to the teacher. Clean up and return shared supplies.

Notebook: Use your own calculation and observed evidence. If you used a supplied-data alternative, say so.

Worked vocational math

For a 36 × 48 in rectangle, find the center and ideal diagonal.

Center offsets = length/2 and width/2. Diagonal² = length² + width².

Center = 18 in by 24 in from the datum. Diagonal = √(36² + 48²) = 60 in.

Digital checkpoints

  1. Record one critical dimension or quantity for this job, with units, endpoints/reference or condition, and its source (measured or supplied). Give your check or one uncertainty. Add the notebook page/date so your teacher can find the full record.
  2. Share one calculation that controls YOUR job: the given values, operation, answer with units, and what the answer tells your builder or inspector. Use your actual design or the assigned classroom case; identify the source. Keep the full drawing and work in your notebook.
  3. A new 30 × 40 in rectangle replaces the model. Give its center offsets and ideal diagonal. Which measurements would you repeat after moving a corner?

Teacher answer key and interpretation

Center 15 × 20 in; diagonal 50 in. Repeat adjacent sides and both diagonals; check moved fixture positions. Keep the tolerance explicitly a classroom criterion.

Inspect, support, extend

  1. For this classroom exercise, sides must be within 1/4 in of the requested lengths and each diagonal within 1/4 in of 60 in; this is an assigned model tolerance.
  2. Show the datum, both fixture coordinates, and the final center.
  3. Explain why a matching pair of diagonals alone does not prove that the requested side dimensions are correct.

Support: Use the scaled 3–4–5 relationship and half-length marks before introducing the square-root calculation.

Extension: Reduce one width by 6 in; recalculate the center and diagonal, then demonstrate the shift.

Individual review

Look for: a checked tool reading; a justified calculation with units; a usable drawing/product; a test-based decision. Record missing evidence as not observed. Give one actionable next step and a chance to revise. Use the phase performance task for a later individual conference.

trades-reset-1.title: Job 04 · Estimate a display surface
trades-reset-1.bodyHtml:
The job

A covering-and-border takeoff with a piece layout and simulated quote.

110 minutes / two periods. Project-based vocational mathematics. Chromebook guides six stages; pocket notebook holds drawings, measurements, calculations, test results, and revisions. Three selected digital responses; no duplicate digital drawing required.

Prepare

Tape, notebook, paper, scissors, pencil, calculator after setting up the math.

Prepare one sample or diagram; approve the work area and verify the model arithmetic before class.

Learning evidence

  1. I can measure from stated endpoints, record units and resolution, and check a reading.
  2. I can calculate lengths, clearances, area, and perimeter with appropriate units.
  3. I can make a dimensioned drawing or work order another person can use.
  4. I can use a fit or inspection result to make and explain a revision.

Use direct observation for tool action and product/drawing evidence. Digital saves and XP are participation records, not mastery ratings. First two jobs establish a baseline: independent / with cue / not observed. Keep existing grading policy; do not turn a group product into every student’s individual rating.

110-minute sequence

  1. 0–12 min · Brief: Point to the surface and then its boundary. Which purchase uses square units and which uses length?
  2. 12–30 min · Measure: Survey a reachable rectangular display area. Record width/height in inches, then convert to feet.
  3. 30–50 min · Plan: Draw and cut the scaled panels and surface. Test that the panel orientation covers the rectangle.
  4. 50–78 min · Make: Assemble a paper proof of the panel layout. Keep offcuts visible.
  5. 78–98 min · Test: Panel count is supported by a layout, not area division alone.
  6. 98–110 min · Explain: Complete the individual exit below before discussing answers.

Brief

  1. Point to the surface and then its boundary. Which purchase uses square units and which uses length?
  2. Set up a dated notebook spread: sketch and readings on the left; calculation, decision, test, and revision on the right. Mark small sketches NTS unless drawn to a chosen scale.
  3. Work in pairs and rotate roles. Each student keeps an individual notebook and performs a tool action and a calculation.

Notebook: Write the job title, date, user/purpose, and your prediction. Keep the Chromebook on the desk while you measure or build.

Measure

  1. Survey a reachable rectangular display area. Record width/height in inches, then convert to feet.
  2. For a shared purchasing exercise, use a model surface 4 × 6 ft. Paper rectangles will represent materials at 1 in = 1 ft.
  3. Separate covering area from border length in two labeled notebook sections.

Notebook: Record readings, endpoints/reference, units, and source. Label values measured, supplied, calculated, or assumed.

Plan

  1. Draw and cut the scaled panels and surface. Test that the panel orientation covers the rectangle.
  2. Make a cutting plan for two 6-ft and two 4-ft border pieces using three 8-ft strips. Show leftovers.
  3. List item, size, quantity, unit price, subtotal, and total. Prices are fictional classroom data, excluding tax and labor.

Notebook: Show operations with units, a labeled drawing, and your work order or decision. Keep original and revised work readable.

Make

  1. Assemble a paper proof of the panel layout. Keep offcuts visible.
  2. Have another pair recalculate quantities from your drawing.
  3. Repeat the takeoff for your measured surface using the same model materials; state any simplifying assumption.

Notebook: Record a build issue or clarification as it occurs. Your product and notebook are the work for this stage.

Test

  1. Panel count is supported by a layout, not area division alone.
  2. The stock plan can actually supply each border piece; no piece is longer than stock.
  3. Quote totals and all units can be traced to the drawing.

Notebook: Record requirement → test/reading → decision → revision → retest. Keep unexpected results; do not invent success.

Explain

  1. Complete the individual exit below before discussing answers.
  2. Add the test result, revision, and notebook page reference to your response. Use the notebook as evidence rather than retyping every page.
  3. Save the three selected responses and submit the lesson for teacher review. Show your physical work and notebook to the teacher. Clean up and return shared supplies.

Notebook: Use your own calculation and observed evidence. If you used a supplied-data alternative, say so.

Worked vocational math

Cover a 4 × 6 ft surface using 2 × 3 ft panels at $4 each. Border comes in 8-ft strips at $3 each. Assume no cutting loss in this paper model.

Area = L × W; perimeter = 2 L + 2 W. Count whole purchasable pieces after checking layout.

Area 24 ft²; four panels tile the surface. Perimeter 20 ft; three 8-ft strips supply 24 ft. Cost = 4×$4 + 3×$3 = $25.

Digital checkpoints

  1. Record one critical dimension or quantity for this job, with units, endpoints/reference or condition, and its source (measured or supplied). Give your check or one uncertainty. Add the notebook page/date so your teacher can find the full record.
  2. Share one calculation that controls YOUR job: the given values, operation, answer with units, and what the answer tells your builder or inspector. Use your actual design or the assigned classroom case; identify the source. Keep the full drawing and work in your notebook.
  3. A 3 × 5 ft board uses 1 × 1 ft covering squares at $0.50 each. Border is sold in 6-ft strips at $2 each; show a feasible plan for two 5-ft and two 3-ft edges. Find covering, border purchase, and total cost.

Teacher answer key and interpretation

15 squares = $7.50; perimeter 16 ft; three 6-ft strips can yield 5, 5, and 3+3 ft. Border $6; total $13.50. Area-only reasoning is insufficient for stock feasibility.

Inspect, support, extend

  1. Panel count is supported by a layout, not area division alone.
  2. The stock plan can actually supply each border piece; no piece is longer than stock.
  3. Quote totals and all units can be traced to the drawing.

Support: Color surface and border differently. Manipulate scaled pieces before dividing.

Extension: Add a 1 × 2 ft opening: compare net area with panel purchase quantity and explain why they may change differently.

Individual review

Look for: a checked tool reading; a justified calculation with units; a usable drawing/product; a test-based decision. Record missing evidence as not observed. Give one actionable next step and a chance to revise. Use the phase performance task for a later individual conference.

trades-reset-1.title: Job 05 · Handle a change order
trades-reset-1.bodyHtml:
The job

A revised tray work order, new prototype, and measured comparison.

110 minutes / two periods. Project-based vocational mathematics. Chromebook guides six stages; pocket notebook holds drawings, measurements, calculations, test results, and revisions. Three selected digital responses; no duplicate digital drawing required.

Prepare

Original notebook/tray, paper, tape, scissors, pencils.

Prepare one sample or diagram; approve the work area and verify the model arithmetic before class.

Learning evidence

  1. I can measure from stated endpoints, record units and resolution, and check a reading.
  2. I can calculate lengths, clearances, area, and perimeter with appropriate units.
  3. I can make a dimensioned drawing or work order another person can use.
  4. I can use a fit or inspection result to make and explain a revision.

Use direct observation for tool action and product/drawing evidence. Digital saves and XP are participation records, not mastery ratings. First two jobs establish a baseline: independent / with cue / not observed. Keep existing grading policy; do not turn a group product into every student’s individual rating.

110-minute sequence

  1. 0–12 min · Brief: A customer changes one requirement. What should stay traceable between the original and revised drawing?
  2. 12–30 min · Measure: Read your original tray dimensions. Mark the original gap and wall height on a fresh sketch.
  3. 30–50 min · Plan: Individually calculate the change to both base and blank for your notebook.
  4. 50–78 min · Make: Trade the revised work order and build a second tray.
  5. 78–98 min · Test: Revision B changes both dimensions by the correct total gap increase.
  6. 98–110 min · Explain: Complete the individual exit below before discussing answers.

Brief

  1. A customer changes one requirement. What should stay traceable between the original and revised drawing?
  2. Set up a dated notebook spread: sketch and readings on the left; calculation, decision, test, and revision on the right. Mark small sketches NTS unless drawn to a chosen scale.
  3. Work in pairs and rotate roles. Each student keeps an individual notebook and performs a tool action and a calculation.

Notebook: Write the job title, date, user/purpose, and your prediction. Keep the Chromebook on the desk while you measure or build.

Measure

  1. Read your original tray dimensions. Mark the original gap and wall height on a fresh sketch.
  2. New requirement: increase clearance from 1/8 to 1/4 in on EACH side; retain 3/4 in walls.
  3. Remeasure the notebook if the original endpoint record is unclear. Preserve the original design as revision A.

Notebook: Record readings, endpoints/reference, units, and source. Label values measured, supplied, calculated, or assumed.

Plan

  1. Individually calculate the change to both base and blank for your notebook.
  2. Make revision B with changed dimensions highlighted and unchanged wall height shown.
  3. Check whether the new blank fits available paper. State whether the paper orientation or joining plan must change.

Notebook: Show operations with units, a labeled drawing, and your work order or decision. Keep original and revised work readable.

Make

  1. Trade the revised work order and build a second tray.
  2. Place original and revised trays side by side with the same notebook.
  3. Record whether the larger gaps satisfy the changed requirement and whether the walls still stand.

Notebook: Record a build issue or clarification as it occurs. Your product and notebook are the work for this stage.

Test

  1. Revision B changes both dimensions by the correct total gap increase.
  2. The builder can identify the current revision and all critical dimensions.
  3. A physical comparison supports the change claim.

Notebook: Record requirement → test/reading → decision → revision → retest. Keep unexpected results; do not invent success.

Explain

  1. I can lay out lengths, centers, and offsets from a common reference.

  3. 30–50 min · Plan: Calculate signed differences and absolute magnitudes for all measured constraints.
  4. 50–78 min · Make: Move a corner or center marker according to the inspection plan.
  5. 78–98 min · Test: Each decision matches the stated tolerance, including the exact boundary.
  6. 98–110 min · Explain: Complete the individual exit below before discussing answers.

Brief

Measure

  1. Lay out a 30 × 40 in rectangle with one deliberately misplaced corner, chosen by the teacher.
  2. Without seeing the planted error, measure all four sides, diagonals, and center coordinates.
  3. Record specified and measured values in separate columns.

Notebook: Record readings, endpoints/reference, units, and source. Label values measured, supplied, calculated, or assumed.

Plan

  1. Calculate signed differences and absolute magnitudes for all measured constraints.
  2. Mark pass/check for each criterion using the teacher’s classroom tolerance.
  3. Propose the smallest correction that addresses the pattern of readings.

Notebook: Show operations with units, a labeled drawing, and your work order or decision. Keep original and revised work readable.

Make

  1. Move a corner or center marker according to the inspection plan.
  2. Remeasure affected sides and both diagonals.
  3. Have the inspecting pair sign a report naming measurements, dates, and remaining limits.

  1. Each decision matches the stated tolerance, including the exact boundary.

Requested length 40 in; measured 40 3/8 in; assigned tolerance ±1/4 in. Decide acceptance.

  2. Both before and after readings are retained.

  3. 30–50 min · Plan: Design a folded beam from the same paper allowance. Dimension fold locations.
  4. 50–78 min · Make: Test flat and folded versions using equal span and centered loading; use fresh matching specimens after permanent creases or damage.
  5. 78–98 min · Test: Data identifies counts, trials, and the failure criterion.

  2. Agree on one loading position at midspan and one loading increment. Use only small loads that stay over the desk.
  3. Record paper, span, load type, support width, and a failure criterion: touches the desk or loses the load.

Plan

  1. Design a folded beam from the same paper allowance. Dimension fold locations.
  2. Predict how the shape changes bending and show where the load travels into supports.
  3. Make a data table for shape, trial, supported count, and observed failure.

Notebook: Show operations with units, a labeled drawing, and your work order or decision. Keep original and revised work readable.

  1. Test flat and folded versions using equal span and centered loading; use fresh matching specimens after permanent creases or damage.

A flat beam holds 2 identical erasers before the chosen limit; a folded beam holds 8. Compare capacity in this specific test.

  1. I can establish and check a reference for a route or elevation measurement.
  2. I can calculate slope, fall, depth, route length, and volume per unit time.
  3. I can draw a coordinated plan and elevation with dimensions and clearances.

  1. 0–12 min · Brief: A tape measures length. How will you know a line is horizontal before calling a vertical difference a rise or fall?
  2. 12–30 min · Measure: On a low desk model, check the spirit level on a stable surface, reverse it end for end at the same location, and compare indications.
  3. 30–50 min · Plan: Draw a side view showing the level reference and both vertical drops.
  4. 50–78 min · Make: Build a low paper route joining the endpoints and check its direction against the reference.
  5. 78–98 min · Test: A horizontal reference is established independently of the tape.

Measure

  1. On a low desk model, check the spirit level on a stable surface, reverse it end for end at the same location, and compare indications.
  2. Use a checked horizontal reference above two endpoints A and B. Measure vertical drops to both points.
  3. Record reference method, endpoint labels, and actual readings.

  1. Draw a side view showing the level reference and both vertical drops.

Drops from one level line are A=2 in and B=3 1/4 in. Which point is lower, and by how much?

Larger downward distance from the same level line means lower elevation.

B is 1 1/4 in below A. A slanted reference line would invalidate this comparison.

  2. Both drops share the same reference.

Fall = run × fall per foot. Percent slope = vertical fall/horizontal run ×100 with equal units.
